question: A teammate runs the assistant twice with the same model and the same question and gets two different explanations of attention. Before suspecting a bug, what should they check first?
options: Whether the model was retrained or swapped for a newer version between the two runs
Whether the question was long enough to overflow the 8,192-token context window
Whether generation samples tokens (do_sample=True) instead of decoding greedily
Nothing: two runs of a language model differ whatever the generation settings

question: In a long chat, a student asks the assistant to repeat word for word a deadline that appeared about 6,000 tokens earlier. Which model is the safer choice for this request, and why?
options: A Mamba-style model, because its fixed-size state does not grow with the chat
Either one, because both read the whole chat and so keep it equally well
A Transformer in its window, because its KV cache keeps every earlier token
An encoder-only model, because it reads the text in both directions at once

question: The university requires that every spoken question to the assistant, and every answer, be stored as text and checked against a policy before the answer is spoken. Which design meets this most directly?
options: A chain of specialists, whose transcript and answer exist as text before any audio
Either design, because both take the same audio in and give the same audio out
One model that hears and speaks, because its lower latency leaves time for the check
A chain of speech-to-text and text-to-speech alone, without a language model

question: Students can send the assistant a typed question, a voice note or a photo of a whiteboard. A teammate proposes that the language model should look at every incoming message and decide which component processes it. What is the main objection?
options: The file type gives the modality, so code routes it for free and identically
None: letting the model decide is the most flexible design, so it is preferable
Language models cannot see file types, so they would misroute the voice notes
A trained classifier would route the messages more accurately than the model

question: The assistant gets a delete_reminder tool. To keep it safe, a teammate adds one line to the system prompt: “Always ask the student before deleting anything.” What is wrong with relying on this?
options: The line asks the model but checks nothing; the approval must be enforced in code
Nothing: models follow their system prompt, which outranks anything in the user’s messages
The line belongs in the user message instead, where the model pays more attention
Deleting cannot be made safe, so the tool must be removed whatever else is done

question: A student reports: the assistant replied “Reminder set for 14 November”, but no reminder ever arrived. Where should the search for the fault start, and why?
options: At the model layer: the model needs retraining, because it wrote a false sentence
At the system layer: the retrieved notes were probably from the wrong lecture
At the agent layer: the log of the add-reminder call, its result, and the store
Outside the assistant: reminders go out by email, which the assistant cannot control

question: Router A costs 0.2 cents per request and routes 80 % of questions correctly. Router B costs 0.05 cents and routes 40 % correctly. What does the cost per successful request say, and what does it leave out?
options: A is cheaper per correct route, because it is right twice as often as B is
The two cost the same per correct route, since price and accuracy cancel out
B is four times cheaper per request, so it is the better choice of the two
B costs half as much per correct route, but the figure leaves out what failures cost

question: In the silver level, 20 reverse steps with seed 1 put 40% of the samples on the ring. You change to 30 steps and get 43%. Can you report that 30 steps improve variety?
options: Yes, provided the mean distance to the shapes did not grow at the same time
Not yet: compare the 3-point change with how much the share moves between seeds
No: more steps make samples cleaner rather than more varied, so the gain is noise
Yes: 43% is closer to the data’s 50% than 40% was, so variety improved

question: A student asks the assistant: “Every Friday at 18:00, summarise what the notes say about the topics of my unfinished to-do items and email the summary to my study group.” Which split of the work follows the lecture?
options: The language model does it all: it can plan the steps, write the summary and send the email
A classifier decides each Friday whether a summary is needed, then sends the email itself
The model tracks the time, writes the summary and sends it when it judges Friday has come
Code fires the schedule and reads the list; the model writes the summary; the email waits for approval

question: To make the assistant’s reminder dates reliable, a teammate switches its controller from sampling to greedy decoding. What does this change, and what does it not?
options: Nothing changes, because decoding affects only the wording, not the tool calls
The same input gives the same output, but a wrong date now repeats on every run
It slows the controller, because greedy decoding scores every token of the vocabulary
It fixes the dates, because the most likely date token is the correct one

question: After the assistant opens to Ukrainian-speaking students, the same kinds of questions start to hit the context limit and use more memory per request. Which explanation follows from the lecture?
options: Ukrainian speakers write longer questions, so each request holds more words
The model needs fine-tuning on Ukrainian before its cache can store Cyrillic compactly
The model puts more attention on the first token in Ukrainian, which wastes memory
The mostly English tokenizer splits Cyrillic into small pieces, so tokens multiply

question: A classmate trains two small models, one on English and one on Ukrainian text, each with its own tokenizer. The English model reaches a loss of 3.2 per token, the Ukrainian one 1.9, and the classmate concludes the Ukrainian model predicts its language better. What should be compared instead?
options: Top-1 accuracy on the next token, since a hit or a miss does not depend on how probable the token was
Nothing: a lower loss per token means better predictions, whichever tokenizer made the tokens
Perplexity per token, since taking the exponential of each loss puts both models on one scale
Total surprise per byte or per character of the same content, since the tokenizers cut it differently

question: Your lab can afford exactly SmolLM2-135M’s training bill, about 1.6 · 10²¹ FLOPs. You want a model with twice as many parameters, about 270 million. How many training tokens does the same budget allow?
options: About 1 trillion: the bill is 6·N·D, so doubling N halves D
About 2 trillion: the bill depends on the number of tokens, not on the model
About 0.5 trillion: the backward pass doubles again for the larger model
About 4 trillion: a larger model needs more data

question: For SmolLM2-135M’s training bill, the Chinchilla balance would have produced a 3.7-billion-parameter model with a lower predicted loss. Why did its makers train a 135-million-parameter model on 2 trillion tokens instead?
options: Because 2 trillion tokens was all the filtered web text they had collected for their pre-training
Because it is run far more often than trained, and per generated token it costs about 27 times less
Because later work showed that the Chinchilla balance asks for far more parameters than a model needs
Because a 135M model trained on 2 trillion tokens reaches a lower loss than the balanced 3.7B one

question: Ukrainian is 1 % of a team’s 1-trillion-token pre-training corpus. To improve Ukrainian, they set its sampling weight to 10 % for a training run of 1 trillion tokens. What happens?
options: Documents in other languages are removed from the corpus until Ukrainian makes up 10 % of it
Nothing changes: the corpus on disk still holds only 1 % Ukrainian, whatever the weights say
Each of the 10 billion Ukrainian tokens is drawn about ten times, with diminishing returns
The model sees 10 % more Ukrainian than before: about 11 billion Ukrainian tokens instead of 10

question: An exam question and its answer were copied onto 300 web pages, each with a different short header, menu and footer. A pipeline removes duplicates by hashing each whole document and dropping documents with identical hashes. How many copies survive, and what would catch them?
options: All 300, since no two pages are byte-identical; MinHash over shingles would catch them
None: the quality filters drop pages of exam questions as low-value text before deduplication
One: the copied question and answer are the same text, so every copy gets the same hash
All 300, and catching them would need an exact comparison of every pair among the 300 pages

question: The assistant must answer questions about university regulations published after its training data was collected. A teammate proposes fine-tuning the instruct model on 2,000 question–answer pairs about the new regulations. What does this section predict?
options: It will not work until the model is pre-trained again from scratch with the regulations
It learns the answers’ form fast and the new facts slowly, and then hallucinates more
It changes nothing, since preference training has frozen the weights fine-tuning would move
It will work: 2,000 examples are plenty for the model to store the new facts reliably

question: The team wants to make the assistant’s small model behave more like a large hosted model that returns only generated text, no probabilities. Which kind of distillation can they do, and what do they give up?
options: Quantization, since rounding the student to fewer bits counts as distillation from its float32 copy
None: distillation needs a teacher and a student with the same architecture and parameter count
Logit distillation, since each generated answer reveals the teacher’s probabilities at every token
Sequence-level: fine-tune on the teacher’s answers, giving up its soft targets at each token

question: In bronze Task 1, the model with less Ukrainian in its data writes eight lines instead of six, mixes in Russian words, and invents details of a recent event. A report explains all three as ‘weak alignment’. What would a better report say?
options: Mixed language: thin Ukrainian data; invented event: cutoff and honesty; line count: instruction following
Mixed language: the tokenizer; invented event: sampling temperature; line count: the knowledge cutoff
All three come from the tokenizer, which splits Ukrainian into bytes and so wastes the model’s context
The report is right: alignment shapes the language, the facts and the format a chat model writes

question: The assistant answers Ukrainian-speaking students poorly, and gets this term’s assignment deadlines wrong in both languages. A teammate proposes one fix for both: DPO on preference pairs in which the correct Ukrainian answers with the right deadlines are chosen. What does the lecture predict?
options: It fixes the deadlines but not the Ukrainian, since the chosen answers write the dates into the weights
DPO fixes neither: deadlines belong in the prompt, and Ukrainian needs pre-training data that cover it
It fixes the Ukrainian but not the deadlines, since preference pairs teach language, not facts
It fixes both: the chosen answers carry the right deadlines and good Ukrainian for the model to learn

question: A teammate argues: ‘For SmolLM2-135M’s training bill, the Chinchilla balance gives a 3.7-billion-parameter model with lower loss. Let us use a model of that size and quantize it to 4 bits, so that it fits the laptop just as well.’ What does the lecture say about this plan?
options: It works: at 4 bits the larger model takes about as little memory and time per token as the small one
It must be measured: 4 bits shrink the bytes, not the arithmetic, which is about 27 times larger
It fails, since quantized models need GPU kernels and cannot run on a laptop’s CPU at all
It works only if the larger model is first pruned by magnitude down to 135 million parameters

question: To choose the assistant’s engine, a team scores several open models by perplexity on the course notes. One model, with a different tokenizer from the others, scores far lower than the rest. Before trusting the result, what should they check?
options: Whether the notes were in its training data, and how it compares in bits per byte, not perplexity
Nothing: a far lower perplexity on the course notes means that this model knows the course best
Whether its perplexity stays this low after quantizing it to 4 bits for the students’ laptops
Whether that model has more parameters, since a larger model lowers perplexity on any text

question: A teammate wants the 135M model to compute the days left until a deadline, and proposes GRPO with a verifier that rewards the correct final number. On the first batch, all eight sampled answers to every question are wrong. Which response follows from the lecture?
options: Keep training: eight wrong answers per question give a strong signal of what to avoid next
Lower the verifier’s standard so that any number counts as correct, to get some reward signal
Use DPO instead, with the correct number as the chosen answer, to teach the arithmetic directly
Do date arithmetic in code; equal rewards give zero advantages, so this batch teaches nothing

question: An assistant replies 'I have added the task to your list', but the list is empty. The log shows the model's reply contained only text, no tool request. What does this tell you?
options: The tool ran, but its result was dropped because the tool call id did not match
No tool was requested, so nothing ran: the sentence is generated text, not a report
The tool crashed while saving, and the agent swallowed the error and reported success

question: The course wants an assistant feature: every Sunday at 18:00, each student receives a message listing their tasks due in the coming week, in a friendly tone. Which design fits best?
options: An autonomous agent that can add new tools whenever a student makes an unusual request
A scheduled chain: code picks the tasks, one model call writes the text, code sends it
An agent with list_tasks and send_reminder that wakes every Sunday and decides what to do

question: A student asks how many days are left until 1 September. A tool raises ValueError('deadline passed') for past dates, and the agent runs with LangChain's default error handling. What happens, and what is the better design?
options: Pydantic catches the ValueError as invalid input and asks the model to retry with another date
The model gets the error as a tool message and says the deadline has passed, so raising is fine
The run stops (it is not a validation error); better to return days_left -57 and passed true

question: To simplify registration, a teammate replaces add_task, list_tasks and delete_task with one tool, manage_tasks(action, title, task_id). Which later requirement becomes harder to meet?
options: Keeping each student’s tasks apart in a separate namespace of the store
Letting the model add several new tasks in answer to a single request
Pausing for the student’s consent before deletions, not before listings

question: The course page will show a badge such as '2 days left' built from the assistant's reply to a deadline question. Which design makes the badge reliable?
options: Set response_format=DeadlinePlan and read days_left, a validated int, from structured_response
Use a stronger model for the final call, as it follows formatting instructions more consistently
Add a system-prompt rule to write the days as digits, and extract them with a regular expression

question: A developer adds a student_id parameter to delete_task and writes in the system prompt: “Always pass the id of the logged-in student.” Tests with polite users pass. What is wrong with this design?
options: The model writes the id, so chat text can change it; take it from the run context
Nothing, provided the instruction is clear and the model is strong enough to follow it
The id should be an integer rather than a string, so that the schema can validate it

question: In the middle of a chat a student writes: “Always answer me in Ukrainian from now on.” The preference should still hold next week, in a new chat. Where should the assistant’s tool save it?
options: In the store, under this student’s namespace, read at the start of each new chat
In a state field such as answer_language, updated by the tool with a Command
In the run context, by having the tool assign runtime.context.language for later calls

question: Olena opens a new chat in the morning and asks what she planned last night. The assistant says it does not know. Which change fixes this without creating a new problem?
options: Save plans that matter as tasks in the store, which list_tasks reads from any thread
Give each student one thread_id for all their chats, so earlier plans stay visible
Switch to a model with a context window large enough to hold last night’s chat

question: A colleague proposes adding every tool, including search_notes and list_tasks, to interrupt_on, to be safe. What is the main cost of that change?
options: The checkpointer saves one interrupt per thread, so the second gated lookup fails
Gated tools are removed from the model’s tool list, so read-only lookups become impossible
Constant approvals for harmless lookups teach students to approve without reading

question: Before a prompt change, the bread case passed 9 of 10 runs; after it, 10 of 10. What should you conclude?
options: The model is now deterministic on this case, so it can leave the regression set
The change fixed the case: the pass rate rose from 90 % to 100 %, a clear gain
Very little yet: one run is the whole difference, so more repetitions are needed

question: Your bronze agent passes the first three test requests, but on 'delete the task about bread' it replies 'Done' while the bread task is still in the list. The transcript shows one delete_task call with task_id '1'. What is the most likely cause, and where is the fix?
options: The store lost the task; switch from InMemoryStore to a persistent database
The model misread the Ukrainian request; translate it into English first
A guessed id: make it list first, and have delete_task report unknown ids

question: For the gold level you run every request three times with a real model. A classmate says one run per request is enough because they set temperature to 0. What is the better argument?
options: Three runs are needed because the scripted model samples its decisions at random
They are right: at temperature 0 the model picks the same tokens, so outputs are identical
Repeats measure how often the agent takes the right path; temperature 0 is no guarantee

question: A university wants an agent that helps staff book rooms. It needs to check availability, book, cancel, and email the organiser. Which design follows from the lecture?
options: A level-6 agent that can create new tools when a booking request does not fit
Separate tools; gates on book and cancel; mail only to the organiser from the login
One tool manage_room(action, room, time, email), so the model has fewer tools to pick from

question: After a model upgrade, students report that the assistant sometimes says a task was deleted when it was not. Tool tests and scripted path tests still pass. Where is the problem, and what is the first check?
options: In the scripted model, which must be updated to match the new version
In the store, which loses deletions; replace InMemoryStore with a database
In the model’s choices; rerun the real-model cases and read the failing traces

question: A teammate proposes storing each student's full chat history in the store, 'so the assistant remembers everything forever'. Which reply uses the lecture?
options: Agree: with the full history in the store, every later chat can recall past details
Refuse: long-term memory makes agents unsafe, so each chat should start empty
Keep chats in threads and save lasting facts, such as tasks and preferences, in the store

question: You decide to precompute a one-paragraph summary of every section of the notes and store the summaries alongside the full text. On which side of the index-time / question-time line does this work fall, and what follows for its cost?
options: Question time — summaries are generated when a question arrives, so the cost grows with the number of questions asked
Index time — each summary is made once per section and reused, so the cost grows with the collection, not the users
Neither — summaries belong to generation, which sits outside retrieval, so their cost is paid with every answer

question: A colleague sets chunk_size=2000 and chunk_overlap=1000 'to be safe'. What is the most likely consequence for the course-notes corpus?
options: Faster search, because overlapping chunks share one vector, so only half of them are scored
Better answers, because each question now brings about four times as much context to the model
Fewer cut facts, but most text is stored twice and results come back as near-duplicate pairs

question: A team stores unnormalised embeddings from a model whose card says 'trained with cosine similarity', then ranks results by raw dot product because it is faster. Passages that are long and emphatic start winning searches they should not. Why?
options: In high-dimensional spaces the dot product is unreliable; Euclidean distance would have ranked these passages correctly
The dot product rewards vector length as well as direction, so longer unnormalised vectors get an unearned bonus
The dot product and cosine give the same ranking, so the bias must come from long chunks matching more words

question: Two retrievers return these top-3 lists for a question: BM25 → [P7, P2, P9], vectors → [P2, P5, P7]. With reciprocal rank fusion (k = 60), which document ranks first, and why does the answer not depend on the two retrievers' score scales?
options: A tie: P2 and P7 each appear in both lists, and RRF counts list memberships, not scores
P2: 1/61 + 1/62 ≈ 0.0325 beats P7's 1/61 + 1/63 ≈ 0.0323; RRF uses ranks, not scores
P7: its first place in BM25 outweighs P2's second, once RRF rescales both score ranges

question: After switching to a new embedding model, recall@5 rises from 0.75 to 0.88, but the fraction of faithful answers falls from 0.90 to 0.80. What has most likely happened, and where should you look?
options: The judge model is miscalibrated, because faithfulness cannot fall while recall@5 is rising
Retrieval improved but generation got worse; inspect the assembled contexts, their order and budget
The new embedding model is worse overall; revert it, since faithfulness matters more than recall

question: Over a corpus of recorded lectures with year and duration fields, a user asks: 'In the 2023 lectures, which ones under 30 minutes cover LangGraph?' Which combination of techniques from this section addresses it, and which single technique would be wrong on its own?
options: HyDE to imagine a short 2023 LangGraph lecture, plus BM25 on "30 minutes"; Multi-Query alone is wrong
Query structuring for the year and duration filters, plus ordinary search on "LangGraph"; HyDE alone is wrong
Multi-Query to reword the question three ways, plus HyDE on the LangGraph topic; query structuring alone is wrong

question: RAG-Fusion raises recall@5 on your test set from 0.81 to 0.88 but triples the latency and the token cost of each question. Which argument is sound?
options: Check which question types gained the seven points, and route only those through RAG-Fusion
Reject it: tripling the cost of every question for seven points of recall is a poor trade
Adopt it for all questions: seven points of recall are worth more than the added latency

question: Your system answers 'Not in the notes' for 30% of questions whose answers are present; for those questions the reranker's top score averages −2.1 (answered questions average +4.3), and inspection shows the correct passage is absent from their reranked top-5. A colleague proposes lowering the gate threshold from 0 to −3. What would that do, and what is the better response?
options: It would let weak evidence reach generation; the gate is flagging a retrieval miss, so fix retrieval
It would have no effect, since the threshold only applies to questions with no answer anywhere in the notes
It would fix the problem: those 30% of questions would pass the gate and get answered again

question: In the bronze homework, a student uses the lecture's default chunking (size 500, overlap 100) and gets seven chunks instead of four. The six answers are still correct. Will the submission pass?
options: Yes — all six answers are correct, and the criteria grade the answers rather than the chunks
No — the criteria require one chunk per company, split at the blank line between companies
Yes, if k is raised from 2 to 3 so that the split facts about each company are all retrieved

question: For the silver level you must write the test set before looking at any results. Why does the order matter?
options: Gold section ids change once the index is built, so the test set must be fixed before indexing
It does not matter: the same questions get written either way, so the scores come out unchanged
Questions written after seeing results drift towards what the system already answers well

question: A legal team indexes 40,000 contract clauses. Questions name clause numbers ('what does clause 14.2 say about termination?') and sometimes paraphrase ('can we exit early without penalty?'). Which retriever design follows from the lecture?
options: Hybrid BM25 and embeddings fused with RRF, contract and version filters, one chunk per clause
Vector search only, with a large embedding model, contract filters and one chunk per clause
Long context: paste each relevant contract into the prompt when a question arrives, with no index

question: After a month in production, your RAG system's faithfulness score drops from 0.92 to 0.78 with no code change and the same pinned embedding, generator and judge models. What changed, and what is the first check?
options: The embedding model degraded in the cache; re-download it and rebuild the whole index
The judge model drifted; replace it with human review of every answer until it recovers
The documents or the user questions changed; first rerun the fixed test set to see which

question: You are asked to add 'chat with the course notes' to the study site, with answers in both English and Ukrainian. Using the lecture, which three decisions must be made before writing code, and in which order?
options: Vector database first, then the prompt, then the embedding model, which is the easiest to swap
Prompt first, then chunking, then the embedding model, since the prompt shapes every single answer
Embedding model first, then chunking to fit its limit, then the store, which is cheapest to swap

question: A shop's assistant answers product questions well but quotes last month's prices, and the price list changes weekly. A colleague proposes fine-tuning it on the new price list every week. What does the measurement point to?
options: Structured output, because a fixed price format stops the model inventing numbers
Fine-tuning every week, because the new prices have to be stored in the weights
Retrieval over the current price list: the failure is stale facts, not behaviour
A larger model, because a stronger model has seen more product catalogues and prices

question: Suppose that after training the small router scores 0.52 on the validation set, against 0.49 for TF-IDF with logistic regression. The router must run offline on students' laptops. What should the team conclude?
options: Ship the trained router: it has the higher score, and only the trained model runs offline
A 0.03 gap on 145 questions is about four questions; first compare per-answer results, latency and size
Discard both, because neither reaches the 0.9 accuracy a router needs before release
Train longer until the validation gap is clearly larger, then report that validation score as the final one

question: A team trains a model to write SQL with GRPO. The reward is 1 if the reply is valid SQL that the database accepts, 0 otherwise. Reward rises steadily during training. What should they check before believing the model improved?
options: Whether each group held at least 64 answers, as in DeepSeekMath, so the advantages are reliable
Whether the queries return the right results on held-out questions, not just valid SQL
Whether the KL penalty was on, because without it a rising reward cannot be trusted
Nothing beyond the curve: a steadily rising reward is the improvement GRPO is designed to produce

question: A teammate proposes adding the source section’s heading to every user message, to give the router more context. Validation accuracy jumps to 0.95. What has most likely happened?
options: The longer prompt spreads the loss over more tokens, which makes the router’s training more stable
The heading names the label’s topic, so the model reads the answer off it; real questions have none
The jump is noise: on just 145 validation questions, gains of this size lie within one standard error
The model now understands the questions better, since the heading adds context it lacked

question: A support team fine-tunes a ticket classifier. Customers often reopen the same issue, so many tickets are follow-ups of earlier ones, and the model will be used for new customers next quarter. Which split measures what they need?
options: Train on all tickets and test on a random 10% of them, so the model sees every category in training
Split by ticket length, putting the longest tickets in test, since they are the hardest to classify
Group by customer, follow-ups with their thread, and put the most recent customers in the test set
A random split of tickets, stratified by category, so the category shares match in train and test

question: A colleague argues: ‘4-bit storage is 8 times smaller than normal, so QLoRA lets us fine-tune a 70B model on our 24 GB GPU.’ What is wrong with the argument?
options: Checkpoints are 16-bit, so 4 bits is 4 times smaller: the frozen weights alone need about 35 GB
The factor of 8 is right, but the LoRA adapters roughly double the size of the model held in memory
Nothing: at 4 bits per weight a 70B model fits in 24 GB, with room left for the adapters
QLoRA trains in 4-bit arithmetic, which needs extra memory to hold the 4-bit gradients

question: A company will serve 12 customer-specific variants of one 7B model from a single GPU, choosing the variant per request. Which training method fits best?
options: Full fine-tuning, because it gives each customer the most freedom
Spectrum, because it trains fewer layers than full fine-tuning
LoRA, kept as 12 separate adapters on one shared base model
Bottleneck adapters, since they add no layers and so no cost per call

question: After training, a teammate reports a validation perplexity of about 1.2 for the router and writes in the release note that the model is excellent, since anything below 10 counts as excellent. What is wrong with this conclusion?
options: It is per-token loss on another scale, set mostly by format tokens, so no band applies; judge by accuracy
The band is wrong: a perplexity of 1.2 counts as excellent just for models under one billion parameters
Nothing: a perplexity this near 1 means the model is almost never unsure, so nearly every route is right
Perplexity should have been computed on the training set, where it is more stable and less noisy than on validation

question: After a month in use, the router has answered 3,000 live questions. To train the next version, a teammate proposes adding all of them to the training data, labelled with the router’s own answers, keeping only those where the top answer was far ahead of the second. What is the best response?
options: Accept: confident answers are almost always right, so they add real-world phrasing at no extra labelling cost
Keep the questions but not the labels: a person labels a sample, close calls first, for the training data
Decline them all: live questions are unlabelled and unvetted, so they would add noise to clean data
Accept, but add them to the test set instead of the training data, since live questions test best

question: A team fine-tunes a vision-language model to read shelf prices from phone photos. Test accuracy is 96 %, yet in the shop the model confidently reports prices for labels that are too blurred to read. What is the most likely cause, and the fix?
options: The vision encoder is too small to see fine digits; replace it with CLIP, which was trained on photos
No training or test photo had an unreadable label; add such photos with an ‘unreadable’ target
The LoRA rank is too low to learn blur; double it, so the adapter has room for the harder images
Too few epochs: train longer, so that the model learns to read the digits on blurred labels as well

question: Whisper is fine-tuned on 2,000 clips from 40 students, split at random into 90 % training and 10 % test clips. Test WER is 6 %. On recordings from next term’s students it is 19 %. What explains most of the gap?
options: WER on next term’s recordings was computed without text normalisation, which inflates the error
The learning rate was too high, so the model overfitted the training clips and generalises poorly
Whisper is an encoder–decoder model and needs far more than 2,000 clips; a CTC model would do better
Every test speaker also had clips in training, so the test measured familiar voices, not new ones

question: Suppose that in the silver level your labelling rule changes the labels of six test questions and you drop two that lean on an unseen passage. The adapter now scores 0.52 on the repaired test set. Can you write that the repair raised test accuracy from 0.49 to 0.52?
options: No: the test set itself changed; score both methods on the repaired set and report it as new
Yes: both numbers are test accuracies of the same router, measured with the same scoring code
Yes, provided the six relabelled questions are excluded when the 0.52 is computed
No, because test questions may not be relabelled once the test set has been used

question: A hospital wants a local model to write discharge letters in a fixed five-part layout, using the patient’s current record and the ward’s in-house abbreviations. The record changes daily. A prompted model gets the layout wrong half the time and misuses some abbreviations. Using the lecture, how should the work be split between repairs?
options: Continue pretraining on the hospital’s records, because the model lacks the language of the domain
Use retrieval for all three problems, since medical text should not be put into a model’s weights
Fine-tune on last year’s letters, so that the model learns the layout, the abbreviations and the facts together
Facts from the record in the input, layout by schema or examples, training for abbreviations if prompts fail

question: A team fine-tunes a ticket router through twelve runs and reaches 0.91 validation accuracy against 0.84 for its keyword classifier. They plan to publish 0.91 and ship the merged model in bf16. Which steps from the lecture are missing?
options: One test run of each method, a check with the adapter off and on, and a score of the merged bf16 file
Retrain once more with a lower learning rate, to confirm that the result holds before publishing
Replace the validation set with fresh questions, repeat the twelve runs on it and publish the best of them
None: 0.91 against 0.84 is a clear win, measured on the set that was used for every choice

question: After a release, students begin to ask some questions in Ukrainian, which the generated training data never contained. The share of close calls in the logs doubles. What does the lecture suggest doing first?
options: Retrain at once on machine-translated copies of the training questions, so the router covers the new language
Raise the LoRA rank, so that the adapter has room to learn a second language next to the first
Label the Ukrainian questions with the router’s own answers and add them to the training data
Have a person label a sample of the Ukrainian questions and measure both methods on them as a group

question: Suppose a colleague compares two LoRA runs on the router: run A ends with validation loss 0.13 and perplexity 1.14, run B with loss 0.17 and perplexity 1.18 but higher validation accuracy. Which run should be kept for the test, and why?
options: Run A, because the loss is computed on more tokens than the accuracy and is therefore more reliable
Run B: the router is judged by the answer it picks, and loss can rise while accuracy improves
Neither: a perplexity above 1.1 on a router shows that both runs failed to learn the task
Run A: lower loss and perplexity mean the model is more certain of its answers, so it is better
